newsitem.title: INDONESIA: East Timor's Belo denies controversial remarks.
newsitem.headline: East Timor's Belo denies controversial remarks.

text.p: Nobel laureate Bishop Carlos Belo on Monday denied accusing Indonesian soldiers of treating residents of East Timor like "scabby dogs" but spoke of terror and intimidation among the people.
Outside his headquarters in the East Timor capital Dili, about 500 students held a pro-independence demonstration and said accusations of ill-treatment by Indonesian troops were true.

Referring to a controversial article published in the German magazine Der Spiegel, the 1996 joint Nobel Peace Prize winner told a news conference that when interviewed he spoke of East Timor's situation since 1976 and not just the present day.

"What I spoke out during the interview does not refer necessarily to my personal views, nor my personal experience as one Timorese or as a priest, but rather as the one in whom people confide deeply...in pouring out their sorrows and pains," Belo said, reading out a statement in English.
"As a bishop I have a moral duty to speak for the voice of the poor and the simple people who, when intimidated or terrorised, cannot defend themselves or make their suffering voiced," he said.

But Belo said he acknowledged the efforts of the Indonesian government in developing East Timor since 1976, the year Jakarta annexed the former Portuguese colony after invading it some months previously.
The United Nations does not recognise Jakarta's rule in the territory and considers Lisbon the administering power.
Der Spiegel published an interview last month quoting Belo as saying Indonesian troops posted in East Timor treated local residents as "scabby dogs" and "slaves".
Belo denied using the word "scabby" and said the interview conducted last April in English and without a tape recorder had been "heavily manipulated and seriously distorted".

"The expression 'scabby dogs' is totally unknown to me. The reason is that I myself did not know the word 'scabby' in English. I came to know of that word only after it was quoted and published in mass media," Belo said.
Belo also denied saying that East Timorese wanted independence.

"I did not make this statement because to the best of my knowledge there are people who are in favour of integration, and there are also still people who still struggle for self-determination," he said. "It is not my intention to defend the integration or independence, but simply to seek improvement in the situation in East Timor."
The Spiegel correspondent has said the interview was taped and has stood by the report.
One student among the protesters outside the building told reporters that they had taken to the streets to show the world Indonesian soldiers were still mistreating East Timorese.
"We have to defend out country. The information in the magazine article is right," the student said. The protesters, shouting "Free East Timor", later dispersed.
Sporadic resistance to Jakarta's rule still erupts in the territory and about 200 guerrillas are said to be still holed up in the rugged hills of the interior.

The troubles in East Timor have grabbed world attention since Belo and self-exiled resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta were jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize last month for their efforts to bring peace to the territory of East Timor.
